overview: Every tile on the map is a terrain, sometimes carrying a feature. Terrain sets the base yields, the movement cost and what can be built; features add to or replace them. A city's first fifteen turns are decided by the six tiles around the settler. Each leader on this roster has ground that suits the kit, and the start bias is the game telling you where it expects the kit to be played.

terrain.name: Grassland
terrain.notes: The most forgiving ground in the game. Farms stack food, and a grassland river is where most capitals want to be. Low production is the cost: pair it with hills or woods.

terrain.name: Grassland Hills
terrain.notes: Food and production on one tile, a defensive bonus and a mine site. The best single tile to settle on: a city on a hill sees further and shoots further.

terrain.name: Plains
terrain.notes: Balanced yields that favour building over growing. Plains with wheat or a river make a production capital; bare plains make a slow one.

terrain.name: Plains Hills
terrain.notes: The production tile. A capital on plains hills builds its first settler five turns sooner. Mines on these win the wonder race.

terrain.name: Desert
terrain.notes: Nothing, until something makes it pay: Desert Folklore, Petra, floodplains, Mali's Suguba or Nubia's pyramids. Desert cities need a river or an oasis to exist and a plan to matter.

terrain.name: Desert Hills
terrain.notes: A mine site in the sand. Petra turns these into the best tiles in the game; without it they are defensible and poor.

terrain.name: Tundra
terrain.notes: One food and nothing else, but furs, deer and the Dance of the Aurora pantheon live here. Russia and Canada are built to settle it; everyone else settles it last.

terrain.name: Tundra Hills
terrain.notes: A hill in the cold. With a Lavra beside it and a mine on it, Russia makes a city here that an ordinary empire could not feed.

terrain.name: Snow
terrain.notes: No yields. A tile to cross, not to work. Oil appears under it late, and Canada can farm beside it; no one else should settle within three tiles of it.

terrain.name: Snow Hills
terrain.notes: One production on a frozen hill. Mines are possible; cities are not worth it unless the Amundsen-Scott station or a late strategic resource is the aim.

terrain.name: Mountains
terrain.notes: Impassable until Mountain Tunnels, but the best neighbour a district can have: +1 Science to an adjacent Campus, +1 Faith to a Holy Site, and the Inca farm them directly with Terrace Farms. Aqueducts draw fresh water from them.

terrain.name: Coast
terrain.appeal: +1 to adjacent land (Breathtaking coast later makes resorts)
terrain.notes: Harbors, fishing boats, sea trade and the Great Lighthouse. A coastal capital grows slower on land but reaches the world sooner. Shallow water takes Harbors; ocean does not.

terrain.name: Ocean
terrain.notes: Deep water, impassable to ships until Cartography. One food and whales, fish or oil. Auckland and the Māori make it productive; for most it is distance.

terrain.name: Lake
terrain.notes: Fresh water without a river: a city on a lake starts with the housing a river gives. Lakes raise appeal and take fishing boats. Nan Madol counts them as coast for its bonus.

terrain.name: Woods
terrain.notes: Production on any terrain, a defensive bonus, lumber mills later, and a chop worth thirty or more production now. Holy Sites gain faith from woods; Campuses do not. Woods regrow with Conservation.

terrain.name: Rainforest
terrain.notes: Food and production with a movement penalty and a hit to appeal. Campuses gain science from rainforest, the Khmer Prasat and Sacred Path gain faith from it, and Brazil's Street Carnival gets its culture from the plantations in it. Chop it or keep it; do not ignore it.

terrain.name: Marsh
terrain.notes: Slow, weak and ugly, until the Lady of the Reeds and Marshes turns each one into two production. Marsh cannot hold a district; clear it with a Builder once Irrigation is known, or plant rice in it.

terrain.name: Floodplains
terrain.expansion: Base Game (grassland and plains floodplains added in Gathering Storm)
terrain.notes: Three food on desert, and floods that pillage improvements and then leave the soil richer. Egypt builds districts on them for free of the flood risk. A Nile start is the best farmland in the game once a dam holds the river.

terrain.name: Oasis
terrain.notes: The one reason to settle open desert: fresh water and three food on a single tile. Cities beside an oasis start with full housing. Cannot hold a district or a farm.

terrain.name: Reef
terrain.notes: A sea tile with production. Campuses gain +1 Science from each adjacent reef, and ships defending on one get a bonus. The Great Barrier Reef counts as reef for every purpose.

terrain.name: Ice
terrain.notes: Impassable sea ice at the poles, which recedes as the world warms in Gathering Storm. It blocks naval routes until the Industrial era melts a passage. Nothing lives here but the Amundsen-Scott station.

terrain.name: Geothermal Fissure
terrain.notes: A vent of heat that a Geothermal Plant can turn into clean power late in the game, and that Hungary's start bias seeks out. Fire Goddess gives it faith. Rare, and worth planning a city around.

terrain.name: Volcano
terrain.notes: A mountain that erupts. Each eruption pillages the ring around it and leaves volcanic soil behind, richer than what was there. Cities two tiles away take the gift and skip most of the damage. Rapa Nui's start bias puts it beside one.

terrain.name: Volcanic Soil
terrain.notes: What an eruption leaves: extra food and production on top of the terrain beneath, stacking with each eruption up to a limit. The reason to settle near a volcano and the reason to keep a Builder close.

glossary.text: Any terrain can be hilly. Hills add +1 Production, cost 2 Movement, give defenders +3 Combat Strength, and let a city see and shoot one tile further. Mines go on hills.

A river runs along tile edges, not through tiles. It gives fresh water (housing), +1 Gold to a Commercial Hub adjacent to it, +2 to a Commercial Hub adjacent to a river and a Harbor, and crossing one mid-attack costs the attacker combat strength. Floods along rivers in Gathering Storm pillage and then enrich.

A tile's attractiveness, from -4 to +4 and beyond. Mountains, coast, woods, natural wonders and Holy Sites raise it; rainforest, marsh, floodplains, mines and Industrial Zones lower it. Breathtaking appeal (4+) allows National Parks and Seaside Resorts, feeds Earth Goddess faith, and grows Neighborhood housing.

A district's bonus from its neighbours. Campus: mountains, reefs, rainforest, other districts. Holy Site: mountains, woods, natural wonders, districts. Industrial Zone: mines, quarries, aqueducts, dams. Commercial Hub: rivers, harbors, districts. Theater Square: wonders, districts. A +3 adjacency district is a historic moment.

Each civilization has terrain it is more likely to start near, in tiers from 1 (strongest) to 5 (weakest). It is a probability, not a promise: Russia usually starts near tundra, Mali near desert, Norway near coast, the Inca near mountains, and a bad roll can give any of them a grassland start.
